content: Countries are encouraged to integrate surveillance activities for viral hepatitis, tuberculosis (TB), HIV, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and other related conditions, particularly among people who inject drugs (PWID). This integration aims to enhance epidemic monitoring and response, improve efficiency, and maximize the return on investment. Surveillance activities must not impose additional burdens on PWID and should undergo ethical review to ensure compliance with human rights standards. Prisons and other congregate settings should be included in national surveillance activities and facility assessments for infection control of TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis. Any newly detected cases during surveillance should be referred to or provided with appropriate care, treatment, and prevention services in line with national guidelines. These individuals should also be connected to drug dependence treatment services, needle and syringe programs (NSPs), mental health and psychosocial care, and drug user groups. This approach extends to prisoners, ensuring access to prison health services and post-release support. Specific guidance has been developed to ensure that HIV surveillance adequately covers key populations, including PWID. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that HIV surveillance be conducted among TB patients and that active TB disease surveillance be conducted among all people living with HIV, regardless of national prevalence rates. This is essential for program planning, implementation, and improving care integration. HIV surveillance among TB patients can be conducted through three key methods: periodic cross-sectional HIV seroprevalence surveys among a representative group of TB patients, sentinel surveys using TB patients as a sentinel group within the general HIV surveillance system, and data from routine HIV testing and counseling of presumptive or diagnosed TB patients. HIV testing should also be integrated into TB prevalence surveys and anti-TB drug resistance surveillance. Surveillance activities must adhere to national guidelines and prioritize the safety and privacy of PWID. Information on drug use status or history must not be shared with law enforcement agencies. Data collected should only be used to improve access to health and social services and to shape national responses to health issues. Ethical principles must be upheld, and the human rights of key populations must be protected. Mapping or identifying PWID populations should be avoided to prevent stigma, arrest, or imprisonment. Full informed consent, privacy, and confidentiality must be maintained during data collection. The involvement of local PWID communities in surveillance activities is critical to ensure the acceptability and safety of the process. This includes engaging PWID networks, peer workers, and civil society organizations in planning, designing, implementing, and monitoring services. Such involvement improves communication and ensures that services are accessible and relevant to the needs of users. National strategic plans for TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, and drug dependence should clearly define the roles and responsibilities of all service providers for PWID. These plans should also ensure the monitoring and evaluation of integrated activities at all levels. Human resource planning must ensure adequate staffing and training to manage TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, drug dependence, and other comorbidities experienced by PWID. Training should include harm reduction principles, patterns of drug use, and the risks associated with drug use, as well as non-discriminatory communication and care practices. Operational research is essential to develop evidence-based, efficient, and effective delivery of integrated services for PWID. Researchers must engage meaningfully with PWID and other stakeholders to address legal, ethical, and regulatory challenges and ensure that research is relevant to the needs of PWID. Ethical research practices must protect participants' human rights, safety, and welfare while being informed by the latest scientific evidence. Countries should establish standardized monitoring and evaluation systems for integrated services for PWID, using harmonized indicators and reporting mechanisms. This ensures that data is captured within national systems and supports the scale-up of comprehensive services to meet global health targets, such as those outlined in the End TB Strategy and UNAIDS goals.
